prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm interested in PlasticWorld, a plastic packaging manufacturer. PlasticWorld makes plastic packaging for beverages, cosmetics, household and automotive chemicals. Its products are top quality — the company has 350 sets of molds with different materials, finishes, and colors, and is always innovating. The overall product mix has not changed in recent years. The sales force is considered 'best in breed'; they hold market share and are compensated based on market share. Two years ago the company invested further in equipment for product innovation. PlasticWorld's customers exhibit strong loyalty and are experiencing increasing pressures in their own industries to innovate plastic packaging.
prompt.question: PlasticWorld's owners are requesting $25M. The offer is final. Should our client buy?

clarifying_info.a: Plastic packaging for beverages, cosmetics, household and automotive chemicals.

clarifying_info.q: How is the sales force compensated?
clarifying_info.a: They are compensated based on market share.
No, the overall product mix has not changed in recent years.

clarifying_info.q: What is the quality of the products?
clarifying_info.a: Products are top quality. Customers are loyal and would continue buying at higher prices.
Two years ago PlasticWorld invested in new equipment for product innovation.
Yes, PlasticWorld's customers exhibit strong loyalty and face increasing pressure in their industries to innovate packaging.

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld P&L Statement in the Past Three Years
exhibits.shows: Three-year income statement (2007–2009) showing Sales ($), Volume (units), COGS ($), SG&A ($), Depreciation ($), and EBIT ($).

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld and Industry Peers Profit Margins
exhibits.shows: Bar chart comparing profit margin (%) for Competitor A through F and PlasticWorld. All competitors show positive margins ranging roughly 5–12%; PlasticWorld's bar falls below zero (approximately –6%).

exhibits.title: PlasticWorld Valuation Sensitivity Analysis
exhibits.shows: Line/curve chart showing company valuation ($M, y-axis 0–50) as a function of profit margin (%, x-axis –10 to 15). Valuation rises as profit margin increases.

framework: Assess current financial performance: calculate profit margin, identify revenue and volume trends
Diagnose root cause of profitability decline: pricing vs. cost vs. mix
Benchmark against industry: determine if problem is company-specific or industry-wide
Estimate realistic achievable profit margin and resulting company valuation
Identify and evaluate feasibility of profit improvement levers
Make buy/no-buy recommendation relative to the $25M ask

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what observations can you make? What is the current profit margin and what is driving the financial trend?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: (1) Calculates profit margin as EBIT/Sales = –$1,176,000 / $18,824,000 ≈ –6% in 2009. (2) Notes volume is growing while revenues are declining — implies average price per unit is falling. (3) Notes product mix is unchanged, so the price drop is not a mix shift. (4) Flags the depreciation jump from $2.25M to $3.45M starting 2008 (equipment investment). (5) Hypothesizes that dropping prices drive the revenue decline despite volume growth. Should ask about reasons for the price drop — leading to the sales force incentive discussion.

math.setup: Profit margin = EBIT / Sales. Price per unit = Sales / Volume.
steps: Price decline: (0.600 – 0.520) / 0.600 = ~13% drop in average price over two years
Volume grew ~10.5% over same period, but revenue still fell
math.answer: Profit margin ≈ –6%; revenue falling because prices are being cut even as volume grows. Depreciation step-up reflects equipment investment.

questions.prompt: What could explain the price drop? (Sales force incentives discussion)
questions.guidance: Strong answer connects the compensation structure to pricing behavior. Sales force is paid on market share, not on earnings or profit. This gives them a direct incentive to cut prices to win or retain customers, even when the high product quality and customer loyalty mean most customers would pay more. Interviewee should independently ask about (or infer) this incentive misalignment. They should also rule out external competitive pressure as the cause, since products are high quality and customers are loyal.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, is this a company-specific problem or an industry-wide issue? What profit margin should be realistic for PlasticWorld?
questions.guidance: The chart shows all competitors (A–F) have positive margins (roughly 5–12%) while PlasticWorld is at approximately –6%. This is clearly a company-specific problem. A realistic target for PlasticWorld, given it has top-quality products and a best-in-breed sales force, is the industry average (approximately 8–10%). At minimum, reaching 0% margin would already represent a significant and achievable improvement.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 3, what is PlasticWorld worth at various profit margin scenarios? How does this inform the buy decision?
questions.guidance: Key read-offs from Exhibit 3: At 0% profit margin, valuation ≈ $25M (breakeven vs. the ask). At industry-average margin (~8–10%), valuation ≈ $40M. Therefore: if the PE firm can bring PlasticWorld to even breakeven profitability, the $25M price is justified. If it can reach industry average, the firm would capture ~$15M of upside. The recommendation depends on whether the profit improvement is feasible and easy to implement.

math.setup: Read valuation from Exhibit 3 sensitivity curve at key margin levels.
math.answer: The deal is attractive if profit margin can be raised to 0% or above; reaching industry average implies ~60% return on the $25M investment.

questions.prompt: What specific changes would you recommend to improve PlasticWorld's profitability? How feasible are they?
questions.guidance: Two primary levers: (1) Change sales force compensation from market-share-based to earnings/profit-based — easy to implement, directly removes the incentive to cut prices. (2) Simplify the product line — eliminate some of the 350 molds to reduce costs and complexity, while leveraging the strong sales force to maintain customer satisfaction. Must be done carefully given customers' demand for innovation. Secondary: examine industry best practices for other improvement areas. Both changes are operational and within a PE firm's control post-acquisition.

brainstorming.prompt: What other areas for profit improvement should the PE firm examine after acquisition?

categories.name: Revenue improvements
ideas: Raise prices to reflect product quality (enabled by fixing sales force incentives)
Upsell premium packaging innovation to loyalty-strong customers
Identify highest-margin products and shift mix toward them

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Rationalize 350-mold product line — eliminate slow-moving or low-margin molds
Renegotiate raw material supply contracts at higher volume
Reduce SG&A by streamlining administrative functions
Investigate COGS efficiency vs. industry benchmarks

categories.name: Organizational changes
ideas: Redesign sales force incentive plan to align with profitability
Introduce pricing governance / approval process to prevent unauthorized discounting
Tie R&D/innovation investment to customer-validated demand rather than blanket mold proliferation

categories.name: Customer strategy
ideas: Segment customers by willingness to pay and target premium segments
Collaborate with key customers on innovation roadmap to reduce speculative mold creation
Introduce tiered service contracts that capture value from loyalty

recommendation: Yes, the PE firm should accept the $25M offer and acquire PlasticWorld

The company is currently worth less than $25M at –6% margin, but two straightforward operational changes — fixing sales force incentives and simplifying the product line — can realistically bring margin to 0% or above, making the deal worthwhile
If industry-average margin (~8–10%) is achievable, the company would be worth approximately $40M, representing ~$15M upside on a $25M investment
risks: Sales force may resist compensation restructuring, leading to turnover or loss of market share
Customers demanding continuous innovation may churn if product line is simplified too aggressively
Depreciation burden from recent equipment investment limits near-term free cash flow
Broader economic or competitive pressures in customer industries could constrain packaging budgets
next_steps: Redesign sales force compensation plan immediately post-close to stop the price bleeding
Conduct a detailed SKU/mold rationalization analysis to identify candidates for elimination without harming key customer relationships
Benchmark all cost lines against industry to find additional quick wins
Set a 12–18 month target to reach 0% margin, with a longer-term plan to reach industry average
